newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa analysts sceptical on Taiwan petchem plan.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa analysts sceptical on Taiwan petchem plan.

text.p: South African oil industry analysts were sceptical on Wednesday about Taiwan state television reports of a plan to invest between $3 billion and $5 billion in a petrochemical development in the country.
"This is news to us. All we know is what we read in the press," said one industry official.
A spokesman for the Mineral and Energy Affairs Ministry said the department had no knowledge of the Taiwanese project.
Trade and Industry spokesman Ismail Lagardien said Taiwan had indicated an interest in a 50-50 joint venture with local industries to establish a petrochemicals plant.

"It is, however, very premature to speculate on the venture because no site has been identified for the project, nor have any details of a deal or of the commercial or industrial aspects been discussed in any way," he said.

Taiwan's state television said on Tuesday that Vice-Premier Hsu Li-teh, currently on a visit to South Africa, would sign a contract worth between $3 billion and $5 billion to build a "petrochemical zone" somewhere in South Africa.
Industry analysts and government sources linked the report to the tussle between Taipei and Beijing for diplomatic recognition by President Nelson Mandela's government.
"Every time their diplomatic status is in doubt, they dangle a carrot like that at us," Minerals and Energy Policy Centre director Rod Crompton told Reuters.
Synthetic fuel producer Sasol Ltd meets Hsu's delegation this week, but spokesman Alfonso Niemand said no investment or joint venture proposals were on the agenda.

Trade and Industry's Lagardien said he was not aware of a rival offer by Beijing, reported by North West Province premier Popo Molefe, of a $12 billion investment over six years in an industrial park a two-hour drive west of Johannesburg.
"Any kind of investment like that would be most welcome and the department would do everything it could to make it possible, but we know nothing about it," he said.
A senior government source said the two bids appeared to be part of the war between Taiwan and mainland China for diplomatic recognition by South Africa.
"A $12 billion investment sounds fantastic -- that's nearly half the annual budget. China is upping the stakes while Taipei's delegation is here in the country," the source said.
Pretoria is the biggest of Taipei's 30 diplomatic allies, but has publicly expressed its desire for ties with Beijing, which demands it sever diplomatic relations with Taiwan first.
Analysts said that a new petrochemicals plant should ideally be situated at Richards Bay, but that there was no refinery there to provide feedstock.
The plant could be built inland at Secunda, making use of feedstock from the Sasol fuel-from-coal utility, but this would make it uncompetitive because of transport costs for exports.
Major oil companies said on Wednesday they had not been approached about feedstock for the petrochemical venture.

Some pointed out that Taiwan funded an inconclusive study into a South African petrochemical plant, possibly involving the ailing Mossgas fuel-from-gas operation, soon after Mandela's African National Congress came to power in 1994.
The then Minister of Mineral and Energy Affairs Pik Botha said at the time that Taiwanese firms could invest billions of dollars, creating hundreds of thousands of jobs.
"Nothing came of that but South Africa continued to recognise Taipei," said one industry analyst.
With Hong Kong due to be transferred to China next year, South Africa has come under increasing pressure to choose between Beijing and Taipei.
Foreign Minister Alfred Nzo has visited Taipei and Beijing and has made a confidential report to Mandela, who must finally decide whether to shift from diplomatic recognition of Taiwan.
Mandela told Hsu during a meeting this week that he wanted to remain friends with both Chinas.
